author: Claude (Opus 5.5), October 17, 2026
run:
A 5-generation run of the current default engine (the feature engine), from Code Zero, with every default setting. It took about 4 minutes and 46 agent calls, and took the evaluator's score from −9.181 (Code Zero, first fit) to **−6.774**: 27.5% of the way to the optimal packing on train, 26.2% on the held-out test split. That's about where run 2 got after 30 generations of the program engine (27.4%), and above run 5 after 10 generations (25.1%).

What the engine does each generation: the **Researcher** reads how the champion packs one instance per family next to a near-optimal packing, and proposes 4 *features* (a feature is a small function that scores every candidate bin). A **Coder** writes each one. At the same time the **Mutator**, which sees only the champion's code and its score, writes 4 more: variants of the champion's features, or fresh ones. **Fit** probes each feature alone on top of the champion at four weights, and if it survives, measures it with versus without (paired refits), on train and on separate validation instances. **Accept** combines the ones that helped on validation and refits the weights. The champion is the weighted sum of the features kept so far.

What actually happened: 40 features were tried and 4 were kept, **all four from the deep loop**. The policy that came out is mostly two ideas: avoid stranding a bin (one resource nearly full while the other has room) and Best Fit (put the job where the bin ends up fullest). Two smaller features about where large jobs go were added in generation 5.

findings.title: The deep loop did all the work; the wide loop kept nothing
findings.text: All 4 kept features came from the Researcher. The Mutator wrote 20 features: 16 were rejected by the probe, 2 helped but were *redundant* (they repeated what the kept features already did), 1 was refuted and 1 was flat. In this run, the wide loop didn't find anything the deep loop then built on, which is the opposite of the "get lucky, then cash in" story.

findings.title: The wide loop isn't wide
findings.text: The Mutator's variant requests are aimed at the champion's own features, ordered by importance. With an empty library (generations 1 and 2) it can only write fresh features, and once one feature existed, 7 of its 9 variants over the next three generations were variants of that same feature (`class_match_residual`, f0013). It has no memory between generations (the air gap also keeps the research log away from it), so it re-proposed a cosine-alignment feature it had already tried: f0004 in generation 1 and f0009 in generation 2 are the same feature, with identical probe results (−14.257 and −26.292).

findings.title: The same idea comes back under a new name, and nothing notices
findings.text:
- Generation 1: f0001 (Mutator) and f0007 (Researcher) are the same measurement, the tighter resource's leftover after placing, and score identically (−0.350). f0005 ranks bins the same way with the sign flipped, and the probe tries both signs, so it scored −0.350 too. Three of eight slots went on one idea.
- f0004 and f0009: the same cosine feature, a generation apart.
- Generation 4's `anticorr_fourth_slot` (f0032) is generation 2's `pair_complementarity` (f0014) with the sign flipped.
- Generation 3's `open_bin_fill_preference` (f0023) is generation 1's f0007 plus a fixed penalty on the new bin.

The research log shows verdicts, but nothing records that two features are the same approach. The probe results are a free fingerprint for this: two features with the same probe scores on the same champion rank bins the same way.

findings.title: The probe decides most features' fate, one feature at a time
findings.text: 30 of the 40 features were rejected by the four-weight probe before any refitting. Each is judged alone on top of the champion, so a feature that only helps next to another one (a tie-breaker, say) can't survive. The mechanisms that would retry those, pair trials and the backlog revisit, are off by default (`--pairs 0`, `--revisit 0`). The search is greedy: one coordinate at a time, kept or dropped.

findings.title: What gets credited is the formula, not the idea
findings.text:
- f0013 is named and argued as *class matching* (does the job's size class complement the bin's leftover shape?), but the measurement written for it is a pure stranding penalty: −(larger leftover − smaller leftover) when the smaller is under 5% and the larger over 25%. The stranding part is what was validated (+1.513), and the log records the class-matching claim as supported.
- f0037's claim says to reward a large job's bin when it ends very tight *or* very roomy, and penalise the middle. Its formula rewards tight and penalises roomy, the Coder said so and implemented the formula literally, and the optimiser then fitted a *negative* weight. So the kept behaviour is the reverse of the formula: for large jobs, prefer bins that keep more than 20% room in both resources. Half of the claim, reached by accident.

The Researcher reads these verdicts next generation as evidence about its claims. Nothing checks that the claim, the measurement and the fitted sign agree.

findings.title: Textbook Best Fit only arrived in generation 4
findings.text: `closing_bin_penalty` (f0031), −(mean leftover after placing), is Best Fit. By the end it's the feature the policy relies on most (importance 5.72, against 1.63 for the stranding penalty). In generation 1 both loops proposed a different best fit, on the *tighter* resource only, which is worse than first fit here (−0.350) because it fills one resource and strands the other.

findings.title: "Stuck" is declared after one generation
findings.text: In generations 2 and 4 the Researcher was told "the policy hasn't improved for 1 generations: the small refinements are used up". In generation 2 the policy was still the empty Code Zero, so there were no refinements to use up. The message fires when `stuck >= 1`, while the extra ideas and the extra Mutator slot start at `stuck >= 2`.

findings.title: There is very little reasoning to see
findings.text: Hidden thinking is switched off (`reasoning_effort: none`), so what you read is all the reasoning there is. The Researcher writes its JSON first, then at most 100 words, in about 8 s. The Coder writes code and one sentence. The Mutator writes code and a name, with no explanation at all. The Researcher's claims are the only place the system says *why*. All thinking levels answer again on Luminal (checked today), so trying thinking for the Researcher alone is now possible and cheap.

findings.title: This isn't the "exaggerate one aspect" design
findings.text: The deep loop doesn't write exaggerated variants of the champion. It proposes a new *measurement* and Fit credits it with the difference it makes, with versus without. The exaggeration probes were the first design and were dropped after runs 1 and 2: the distorted copies always scored worse and crowded the pool (HANDOFF.md §9). If you want probes that exaggerate one aspect to learn about it, that's a change to build, not something the current code does.

findings.title: Fitting time grows when things go well
findings.text: Generations 1 to 4 took 13-32 s. Generation 5 took 152 s, 150 of them fitting: five features passed validation, so combining them, the joint refit and two second-chance retries all ran. The agents' time stayed at about 10 s per generation throughout.

generations.0: Code Zero goes into the library. The library is empty, so every bin scores 0 and each job goes into the oldest bin it fits: first fit, −9.181.
generations.1: Nothing kept. The Researcher saw two failures in the packings (stranded bins in large, bimodal and anticorr; missing 4-job bins in anticorr) and proposed four features about leftovers after placing. The Mutator, with no features to vary, wrote four fresh ones. All eight were rejected by the probe. Three of them were the same idea (prefer the bin whose tighter resource ends fullest), which is worse than first fit here.
generations.2: The big jump: −9.181 to −7.356 (20.8%). The Researcher, reading that balance-only ideas had failed, proposed four features that condition on the arriving job. One of them, written as a stranding penalty, gained +1.83 on train and +1.51 on validation. The Mutator again wrote four fresh features (still nothing to vary), one of which repeated a generation-1 feature exactly.
generations.3: Nothing kept. The Mutator now had one feature to vary and spent four slots on it (three variants of the stranding penalty, one fresh); all rejected by the probe. The Researcher, through the lens of *open a new bin or use an open one*, proposed four features; one was a repeat of a generation-1 idea plus a penalty on the new bin. All eight rejected by the probe.
generations.4: −7.356 to −7.125 (23.5%). The Researcher noticed that the champion never finishes a bin (12-14% left in both resources in large) and proposed −(mean leftover after placing), which is Best Fit: kept, +0.38 train, +0.18 validation. Its other three ideas, including a sign-flipped repeat of generation 2's pair_complementarity, were rejected by the probe, as were all four Mutator features (three variants of the stranding penalty, one fresh).
generations.5: −7.125 to −6.774 (27.5%). Five features passed validation: three from the Researcher and two Mutator variants. Combined greedily, two Researcher features joined (both about where large jobs go); the rest were redundant with them. Second chances for two near-misses found nothing. Fitting took 150 s of the generation's 152.

calls.c005: Generation 1, Code Zero as the champion. It read the packings and named two failures: stranded bins (55 in large and 104 in anticorr, against 2 and 0 for the near-optimal packing) and anticorr stopping at 3-job bins where the optimum builds 4-job ones. It proposed four features, all measured on the leftover after placing: balance between the two leftovers, the tighter leftover (tightest fit), slack on the job's light resource minus its heavy one, and "room for another job". It said plainly that the champion never compares bins at all, so every idea is about comparing them.
calls.c014: Generation 2. It read the log (generation 1's balance-only features all failed) and concluded they failed because they ignored the arriving job. All four new ideas condition on the job: penalise bins this job would strand (class_match_residual, the one that worked), match the job's demand profile to the bin's leftover profile (bimodal), count how many more copies of a small job still fit, and pair CPU-heavy jobs with bins that have memory slack (uniform). It was also told the small refinements were used up, which wasn't true yet.
calls.c023: Generation 3, through the lens of opening a new bin or using an open one. It saw large and anticorr bins closing at 2 jobs with 12-14% left in both resources, and proposed: prefer topping up a nearly full bin over opening (a repeat of generation 1's tightest-fit idea, plus a penalty on the new bin), reward imbalance only while it's still usable, absolute slack for tiny jobs, and a ratio form of tightness. All four were rejected by the probe.
calls.c033: Generation 4. Its key observation: the champion *never finishes a bin*; in large it closes bins with 12-14% left in both resources, where the optimum leaves 3% and 0%. That gave closing_bin_penalty, −(mean leftover after placing), which is Best Fit, and it was kept. The other three: a skew-matching feature for anticorr (generation 2's pair_complementarity with the sign flipped), keeping room for a second large job in bimodal, and piling small jobs into the fullest bin.
calls.c042: Generation 5, through the lens of job size classes sharing a bin. A single theme across four families: the policy treats each job as a one-off fit and never asks whether the bin can still take another job of the same class. Four features: room for a second large job (big_with_big_room_penalty, kept), room for a fourth small job in anticorr (redundant), a large job closing a bin cleanly or leaving room for another large one (bimodal_small_slot_for_large, kept, though its formula contradicts that sentence), and room for a same-size repeat in uniform (flat).

features.f0001: Mutator, fresh: prefer the bin whose tighter resource ends up fullest after placing (−min of the two leftovers). The same measurement as the Researcher's f0007 in the same generation. Worse than first fit by 0.350 at every weight, so rejected by the probe.
features.f0002: Mutator, fresh: signed imbalance of the leftovers, scaled by how full the bin would be. Catastrophic at both signs (about −42); rejected by the probe.
features.f0003: Mutator, fresh: an estimate of the thin, unusable strip a job leaves in a bin. Rejected by the probe (−1.533 at best).
features.f0004: Mutator, fresh: cosine between the bin's remaining room and the job's demand (a Tetris-style alignment). Rejected by the probe (−14.257). Re-proposed a generation later as f0009, with identical results.
features.f0005: Researcher's "room for another job": the tighter leftover after placing, minus 0.5 if that falls under 20%. With the sign the optimiser prefers, it ranks bins exactly like f0001 and f0007 (−0.350 at the good sign), so it was the third copy of one idea in this generation.
features.f0006: Researcher's complementarity idea for anticorr: slack on the job's light resource minus slack on its heavy one. Rejected by the probe (−10.607 at best): it sends jobs to bins that suit their shape regardless of how full they are.
features.f0007: Researcher's "tightest fit": −(the tighter leftover after placing). It expected denser bins in large and bimodal; it scored −0.350, because filling one resource strands the other. The same measurement as f0001.
features.f0008: Researcher's balance idea: −|CPU leftover − memory leftover| after placing, to stop stranding. Alone it's much worse than first fit (−3.433); it never got to be tried next to a fullness feature.
features.f0009: Mutator, fresh: cosine alignment again, the same feature as f0004 from generation 1 (identical probe scores). The Mutator has no record of what it tried before.
features.f0010: Mutator, fresh: the geometric mean of the two leftovers, divided by the job's own size. The only Mutator feature in generations 1-2 to pass the probe (−0.061 at the good sign), but it lost 0.522 on validation: refuted.
features.f0011: Mutator, fresh: smaller leftover minus the gap between the two (a balance score). Rejected by the probe (−4.326).
features.f0012: Mutator, fresh: how much the bin's scarcer resource gets used, plus half the imbalance. Rejected by the probe (−1.876).
features.f0013: **Kept, generation 2: the run's biggest gain** (+1.828 train, +1.513 validation). Named and argued as class matching, but the code is a stranding penalty: score −(larger leftover − smaller leftover) for a bin this job would leave with under 5% in one resource and over 25% in the other, 0 otherwise. Fitted weight +0.38. It's still the second most important feature at the end.
features.f0014: Researcher's complementary pairing for uniform: −(bin leftover skew × job skew), to put CPU-heavy jobs where memory is plentiful and vice versa. Rejected by the probe (−11.459). It came back with the sign flipped in generation 4 (f0032).
features.f0015: Researcher's small-job density: for small jobs only, how many more copies of this job the bin could still take. Rejected by the probe (−0.292 at best).
features.f0016: Researcher's demand-profile match for bimodal: need-weighted average leftover minus the larger leftover. Rejected by the probe (−4.795).
features.f0017: Mutator, fresh: signed, normalised leftover imbalance scaled by fullness. Catastrophic at both signs (about −36).
features.f0018: Mutator, variant of the stranding penalty: a softer, graded version (soft thresholds instead of 5%/25% cut-offs). Worse than the champion at every weight (−1.748 at best).
features.f0019: Mutator, variant of the stranding penalty: how much the placement worsens the imbalance, relative to the job's size. Its first version returned the wrong shape and was repaired (call c028); the repaired version lost 0.101 at best, so rejected by the probe.
features.f0020: Mutator, variant of the stranding penalty with soft ramps and extra weight for jobs that are big in one resource only. Rejected by the probe (−0.552).
features.f0021: Researcher's "imbalance is fine while still usable": −|gap| + larger leftover when the smaller is over 5%. Rejected by the probe (−1.743).
features.f0022: Researcher's absolute tight-side slack for tiny jobs, with the new bin always last. Rejected by the probe (−3.425).
features.f0023: Researcher's "top up a nearly full bin rather than open one": −(tighter leftover), minus 1 for the new bin. Generation 1's tightest-fit idea (f0007) with a penalty on opening. The closest miss of the generation (−0.081), but still rejected by the probe.
features.f0024: Researcher's ratio form of tightness, tight/(tight + 0.05), with the new bin set to 0. Rejected by the probe (−7.923).
features.f0025: Mutator, fresh: tighter leftover divided by looser leftover. Rejected by the probe (−1.367).
features.f0026: Mutator, variant of the stranding penalty, scaled by how full the bin already is. Rejected by the probe (−0.552).
features.f0027: Mutator, variant of the stranding penalty, weighted by how much the leftover's skew differs from the job's own skew. Rejected by the probe (−2.270).
features.f0028: Mutator, variant of the stranding penalty, signed by which resource is left tight. Rejected by the probe (−0.686).
features.f0029: Researcher's "keep bins open for a second large job": for large jobs only, the tighter leftover after placing, 0 for the new bin. Rejected by the probe (−0.554).
features.f0030: Researcher's "pile small jobs into the fullest bin": for small jobs, −(sum of leftovers), new bin last. Rejected by the probe (−15.554). The new bin was set to −1, but a nearly empty open bin scores close to −2, so small jobs preferred opening a new bin over any open bin less than half full.
features.f0031: **Kept, generation 4** (+0.379 train, +0.183 validation): −(mean of the two leftovers after placing), which is Best Fit. It came from the Researcher noticing that the champion never finishes a bin. Fitted weight +0.87, and by the end it's the most important feature (importance 5.72).
features.f0032: Researcher's skew-matching for anticorr: leftover skew × job skew. Exactly generation 2's pair_complementarity (f0014) with the sign flipped, and the probe tries both signs, so this was the same test again. Rejected (−13.633).
features.f0033: Mutator, variant of Best Fit: fill the binding resource, minus half the imbalance. Exactly no effect at small weights and lost a little on validation: flat.
features.f0034: Mutator, variant of the stranding penalty with soft thresholds, weighted by how lopsided the job is. Helped alone (+0.084 validation) but added nothing once the generation's two kept features were in: redundant.
features.f0035: Mutator, fresh: which resource is the bottleneck after placing, signed, scaled by tightness. Rejected by the probe (−0.231).
features.f0036: Mutator, variant of Best Fit that weights nearly sealed bins more (1/(tight + 0.1)). The best Mutator feature of the run (+0.116 train, +0.126 validation), but redundant next to the kept features.
features.f0037: **Kept, generation 5** (+0.203 train, +0.070 validation). For large jobs only. The claim was: reward bins that close cleanly or keep room for another large job, penalise the middle. The formula instead rewards tight and penalises roomy (the Coder flagged this and followed the formula), and the optimiser fitted a weight of −0.45, reversing it. What the policy uses: for large jobs, prefer bins that keep more than 20% room in both resources.
features.f0038: Researcher's "room for a same-size repeat" for uniform: how many more jobs of this exact size fit in the tight resource. Flat on validation (−0.005); its second chance next to the kept features lost badly (−1.593).
features.f0039: Researcher's "room for a fourth small job" in anticorr: +tighter leftover if both resources keep 20%, else −tighter leftover (the Coder read one term differently from the text and said so). Helped alone (+0.060) but redundant next to the kept features.
features.f0040: **Kept, generation 5** (+0.264 train, +0.161 validation). For large jobs only: the leftover on the job's heavy resource minus the other one, counted only while both keep over 20%. In effect it keeps room for another job heavy in the same resource, as the Researcher intended (2LL bins in large). Fitted weight +0.22.
